title: Coastal Karnataka's Ancient Food-as-Medicine Tradition Is Vanishing, Workshop Warns
excerpt: At a workshop near Mangalore, scholars and food creators say traditional dishes calibrated to seasonal health needs are being lost to steel vessels and gas stoves.
body:
• A workshop at Mangalore's Rani Abbakka Tulu Museum highlighted the rapid erosion of Tulu Nadu's traditional food culture, shaped by centuries of coastal living.
  • Coastal Karnataka's cuisine changes with seasons and serves as indigenous preventive medicine, according to a retired Mangalore University professor.
  • Traditional cooking methods using clay pots and wood fires produce flavors that modern kitchens cannot replicate, speakers warned.
  • Food vloggers and cultural institutions are now racing to document vanishing recipes before they are lost to the next generation.

Food as Seasonal Medicine

The food culture of coastal Karnataka is not just about taste — it is a system of preventive health care built over centuries, according to speakers at a workshop on disappearing Tulu Nadu food traditions held at B.C. Road near Mangalore on Saturday.

B. Shivarama Shetty, a retired professor from Mangalore University's SVP Institute of Kannada Studies, told the workshop that the region's traditional diet changes with the seasons, with each dish calibrated to the body's needs at that time of year.

"The food that is consumed not only fills the belly but also acts as medicine."

— B. Shivarama Shetty, retired professor, Mangalore University

Dr. Shetty pointed to Aati Kashaya, a herbal preparation consumed during the current monsoon season, as an example of food with documented medicinal properties. The drink, made from a blend of local herbs and spices, has been part of the regional diet for generations.

Flavors That Modern Kitchens Cannot Match

Writer Rajashri Perla noted that food traditions vary even within the coastal strip. The cuisine of communities living on the plains differs from those near the coastline and those in the Western Ghat highlands, she said.

Perla made a point that would resonate with anyone who has tried to recreate a family recipe in a modern kitchen: the traditional methods of preparing dishes — using clay pots, wood-fired stoves, and time-tested techniques — produce flavors that steel vessels and gas stoves simply cannot replicate.

Vloggers Race to Document What Remains

Sudarshan Bhat Bedradi, a popular food vlogger from Kasaragod in Kerala, said he has been creating videos on traditional coastal dishes and sharing them on social media to bridge the generational gap.

"I show the traditional way of preparing dishes to the present generation, who is largely disconnected from these methods," Bedradi said. During the Aati season, when heavy monsoon rains blanket the coast, traditional cooks turn to leaves, sprouts, cucumber, banana, and jackfruit seeds as primary ingredients — dishes specifically designed for the damp, cool conditions.

Purushottam Adve, an artiste who comes from a family of traditional cooks, struck a more optimistic note: the younger generation would embrace these foods once they understood the health benefits.

A Culinary Heritage Under Pressure

Tulu Nadu, the coastal belt spanning Mangalore, Udupi, and parts of northern Kerala's Kasaragod district, is home to one of India's most distinctive regional food traditions. Coconut, curry leaves, and fresh seafood form the backbone of a cuisine shaped by the Arabian Sea to the west and the Western Ghats to the east.

Iconic dishes like Kori Rotti — chicken curry served with crispy rice wafers — and Neer Dosa, paper-thin crepes made from rice and water, have gained recognition well beyond the region. Udupi's temple kitchens spawned a vegetarian tradition that powered thousands of restaurants across India and overseas.

But the everyday home cooking tradition — the seasonal preparations, the fermented foods, the medicinal herbal drinks — is fading as urbanization changes how families cook and eat. The workshop, organized by the Rani Abbakka Tulu Adhyayana Kendra in association with the India Foundation for the Arts, signals that efforts to document and preserve this heritage are gaining institutional support.

For the large Mangalorean and Tulu diaspora, the findings are a reminder that even in the food's homeland, these traditions are no longer a given.
